claims.text: The initial HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a yield strength of 786 MPa.
The initial HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The initial HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a terminal tensile strain of 13.5%.
HfZrTiTa0.53 should be annealed at 850 °C for 1 hour and rapidly water-quenched.
The specified heat treatment will refine the grain structure.
The specified heat treatment will produce a dual-phase microstructure through controlled phase partitioning.
Grain refinement can improve ductility by promoting more uniform plastic deformation.
A softer phase alongside a retained strengthening phase will improve strain accommodation and uniform tensile deformation.
The treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation by at least 30%, from about 13.5% to at least about 17.5%.
The treated alloy will retain a yield strength near 786 MPa.
The treated alloy will retain a compressive strength near 1314 MPa.
The treated alloy will retain similar impact-triggered chemical-energy release.
Related thermomechanical treatments in multicomponent alloys have produced improved ductility while retaining high strength.
The predicted improvement applies at room temperature under quasi-static tensile loading at approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
Effects at elevated temperature, extreme strain rates, or under additional processing variations are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% baseline is identified as terminal tensile strain in the initial-state fields but is subsequently treated as uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct tensile metrics, so the claimed change from 13.5% to 17.5% does not use a consistently defined baseline.

The experiment calls for tension, compression, and impact tests under identical loading conditions while specifying quasi-static loading near 10^-3 s^-1 and excluding extreme strain rates. An impact test is dynamically loaded and therefore cannot literally share the same loading mode and strain rate as the quasi-static tests.
